twoModels.headline: Confirmed by two independent models, not just one.
twoModels.subhead: Every insight is checked against a second, independent analysis. When both agree, you know it's solid. When they don't, you see exactly where and why.

confirmed.title: Confirmed by both models
confirmed.body: A long-standing low vitamin D reading is flagged consistently by both the evidence-based and contextual analysis.
confirmed.caption: This is what most insights look like.

differs.title: The two models see it differently
differs.body: One analysis emphasizes the sustained lab pattern; the other weighs how recent schedule and sun exposure shape the same finding.
differs.caption: This happens occasionally, and you see both sides when it does.
differs.evidenceReasoning: Persistent low 25-OH vitamin D across repeated labs supports a clear deficiency signal.
differs.contextualReasoning: Recent indoor work months and limited outdoor time may explain the same low reading without implying a lasting metabolic issue.

linkage.label: Data linkage
linkage.title: Link questionnaire data to unlock dual opinion
linkage.body: Health Guide compares an evidence-based view with a contextual view once enough questionnaire sections are linked into your Human Data Model.
linkage.caption: Example based on a common health question about afternoon energy — illustrative sample content, not your personal data.
linkage.question: Why do I feel drained after lunch?
linkage.chipHint: Toggle sections to change linkage completeness.
linkage.lockedBody: Link at least 40% of questionnaire sections to unlock the side-by-side Health Guide comparison.

opinionA.summary: Afternoon energy decline is linked to circadian rhythm and postprandial glucose response.
reasoning: Circadian rhythm naturally dips between 1–3 PM (adenosine accumulation).
Postprandial glucose fluctuations affect alertness (insulin response).
Meal composition directly impacts blood sugar stability.

recommendations.title: Optimize meal macronutrient balance
recommendations.description: Aim for protein, complex carbs, and fats at lunch to stabilize glucose for several hours.

recommendations.title: Strategic light exposure
recommendations.description: Get 10–15 minutes of bright natural light after lunch to support alertness.

recommendations.title: Brief movement protocol
recommendations.description: A short post-meal walk can improve glucose handling and reduce the afternoon dip.

opinionB.summary: Your afternoon energy dip is likely a mix of meal timing, stress load, and habits you can adjust practically.
reasoning: Lunch timing and composition affect how you feel afterward.
Work environment and stress levels play a role.
Small behavior changes can create noticeable improvement.
Individual response varies — what works must fit your day.

recommendations.title: Mindful eating practice
recommendations.description: Take a few unhurried minutes at lunch without screens to ease digestion and the post-meal crash.

recommendations.title: Power posture break
recommendations.description: Around mid-afternoon, stand, stretch, and take several slow breaths as a simple reset.

recommendations.title: Hydration check
recommendations.description: Drink water with lunch and again mid-afternoon — dehydration often feels like fatigue.

agreements.consensus: Both views support light activity after lunch to steady energy.
Both note that what and how you eat at lunch affects the afternoon dip.

disagreements.explanation: The evidence-based view leads with metabolic meal structure; the contextual view leads with how you eat under real-day stress.
